(Surah 20: Ta-Ha)

Makkan, and it has one hundred and thirty-five verses.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Ta-Ha.﴾ Qalun, Ibn Kathir, Ibn Amir, Hafs and Ya'qub read it with emphatic (fakhkham) pronunciation according to the original form, while Abu 'Amr and Warsh alone emphasize the ta' (ṭāʾ) because of its emphatic quality (istiʿlāʾ), and the rest read both with imala (inclination). They are among the names of the letters. It has also been said that its meaning is "O man" in the dialect of 'Akk. If this is correct, then its original form may have been "ya hadha," and they manipulated it through transposition (qalb), abbreviation (ikhtisar), and the citation of the verse:

Indeed, the foolishness of your characters has been "ṭāhā"... may Allah not sanctify the characters of the accursed.

This view is weak, since it is possible that it is an oath, like His saying ﴿Ha, Mim. They will not be helped.﴾ It has also been read as ﴿Ta-Ha﴾ as a command to the Messenger ﷺ to tread the earth with his two feet, for he used to stand in his night prayer on one of his feet. Its original form was "ṭa'", and its hamza was changed to a hā', or in yaṭa'u it was changed to an alif, as in His saying: "No, there is the pasture." Then the imperative was formed from it and the pause particle hā' was added to it. On this basis it is possible that the original form of Ta-Ha was "ṭa'hā," with the alif replacing the hamza and the hā' referring to the earth. However, this is refuted by the fact that they are written in the form of letters, and likewise by the interpretation "O man," or by limiting it to the two halves of the words and referring to them by their names.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verses 2–3:

﴿We have not sent down the Qur'an to you that you should be distressed﴾. The predicate (khabar) of ﴿Ta-Ha﴾ is this clause, if you make ﴿Ta-Ha﴾ a subject (mubtada') with the understanding that it refers to the surah or to the Qur'an, and the Qur'an here occupies the place of the returning pronoun (ʿaʾid). Its answer (jawab) is this clause, if you make ﴿Ta-Ha﴾ an oath (muqsam bihi) or a vocative (munada) addressed to the Prophet, if you make it a vocative call (nida'). It is a resumptive sentence (istiʾnaf) if the clause is a verbal or nominal sentence, with an implied subject (mubtada') omitted. Or ﴿Ta-Ha﴾ is a group of letters quoted as they are (mahkiyya). The meaning is: We have not sent down the Qur'an to you so that you should exhaust yourself through excessive grief over the disbelief of Quraysh, since your duty is only to convey the message; or through excessive exertion, excessive night prayer and standing on one leg. The word al-shaqa' (distress, hardship) is commonly used in the sense of fatigue, and from it comes the saying "more wearied than the colt being broken in," and "the leader of the people is their most wearied (ashqahum)." Perhaps He chose this word to convey that the Qur'an was sent down to him so that he would be happy. It has also been said that this is a refutation and denial of the disbelievers, for when they saw how much he worshipped, they said: "Indeed you are distressed by abandoning our religion, and the Qur'an was sent down to you so that you would be distressed by it."

﴿But as a reminder﴾. The word illa here means "but" (lakin), and tadhkira is in the accusative as a discontinuous exception (al-istithna' al-munqati'). It cannot be a substitute (badal) for the place of ﴿to be distressed﴾, because the two categories differ. Nor can it be an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu) for ﴿We have sent down﴾, because a single verb does not transitively govern two causes. It has also been said that it is a verbal noun (masdar) in the position of a circumstantial state (hal) from the kaf (you) or from the Qur'an, or an object of purpose, with ﴿to be distressed﴾ being attached to an omitted element which is an attribute of the Qur'an, meaning: We have not sent down to you the Qur'an that was sent down so that you would be fatigued by conveying it, except as a reminder. ﴿For whoever fears﴾: for the one in whose heart there is fear and tenderness that is affected by warning, or for the one whom God knows will fear, through being warned by it, for he is the one who benefits from it.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 4:

﴿تَنْزِيلا﴾ is in the accusative, either by supposing a verb governing it, or by (taking it as governed by) ﴿يَخْشى﴾ (He who fears), or in the sense of praise (al-madh) or as an apposition (badal) of ﴿تَذْكِرَةً﴾ (a reminder), if the latter is made a circumstantial clause (hal).

But if it is made an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), either verbally or in meaning, then it is not permissible, because a thing cannot be the cause of itself, nor of its own kind. ﴿مِمَّنْ خَلَقَ الأرْضَ والسَّماواتِ العُلا﴾ (from He who created the earth and the lofty heavens), together with what follows up to His words ﴿لَهُ الأسْماءُ الحُسْنى﴾ (His are the most beautiful names), is an exaltation of the status of what is sent down, through the great magnification of the One who sent it down, by mentioning His acts and attributes in the order that is natural to reason. He began with the creation of the earth and the heavens, which are the foundations of the world, and placed the earth first because it is closer to the senses and more evident to them than the lofty heavens. (Al-'Ulā is the feminine plural of al-A'lā.) Then he indicated the manner in which the existents came into being and the management of their affairs, by intending the Throne (al-'Arsh), from which he sent forth the judgments and decrees, and from which he sent down the causes in an order and in measures according to what His wisdom required and what His will was attached to. Thus He said:

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 7:

﴿And if you speak aloud, then indeed He knows the secret and what is yet more hidden.﴾ That is: and if you speak aloud in the remembrance of Allah and in supplicating to Him, then know that He is free of need of your loudness, for indeed He, glory be to Him, knows the secret and what is more hidden than it, namely the innermost thought of the soul (ḍamīr al-nafs). In this there is a reminder that the prescribing of remembrance (dhikr), supplication (du'ā') and loud utterance in matters where the purpose is not to inform Allah, but rather to form the soul through remembrance, to firmly fix it in the soul, to restrain it from occupying itself with other than Him, and to humble it through supplication and entreaty (tadarru' wa-al-judār).

Then, since it has become clear through this that He is the one who combines the attributes of divinity (ṣifāt al-ulūhiyyah), He made clear that He is the one who is singular in them and the one who is unique in what they entail, so He said:

﴿Allah—there is no god but Him. To Him belong the Most Beautiful Names.﴾ The word "man" in ﴿of the One who created the earth﴾ is a *sila* (relative clause, a complement that completes the meaning of a relative word) attached to ﴿revelation﴾, or it is an adjective (*sifa*) describing it. The shift from the first person (*takallum*) to the third person (*ghayba*) is for variety of expression (*tafannun*) and to magnify the One who sent down the revelation, in two respects. The first is attributing its sending down to a pronoun for the One of great majesty. The second is ascribing it to the One who is characterized by the attributes of majesty and generosity, and it alerts the listener that it is obligatory to believe in it and submit to it, because it is the speech of One of such a stature. It is also permissible that ﴿We sent it down﴾ be a quotation of the speech of Gabriel and the angels who descended with him.

It is read in the genitive, ﴿the Most Merciful﴾, as an adjective of "the One who created", and then ﴿established Himself upon the Throne﴾ is a deleted predicate (*khabar mahdhuf*). The same applies if ﴿the Most Merciful﴾ is put in the nominative as a expression of praise, not as a subject (*mubtada'*). It is also permissible that it be a second predicate.

Al-thara (the dust) is the earthen layer of the earth, which is its last layer. Al-husna is the feminine form of al-ahsan (the most excellent). The superiority of Allah's names over all other names in excellence is because they indicate meanings that are the most noble and the most excellent of meanings.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verses 9–10:

﴿Has the story of Musa reached you?﴾ He (Allah) preceded the preparation of his (ﷺ) prophethood with the story of Musa, so that he might follow his example in bearing the burdens of prophethood, conveying the message, and being patient in enduring hardships, for this surah is among the first to be revealed.

﴿When he saw a fire﴾: this is a time adverbial (ẓarf) relating to ﴿story﴾, because it is an event (ḥadath), or it is an object (maf'ūl) of ﴿remember﴾. It is said that he asked Shu'ayb, peace be upon them both, for permission to leave to visit his mother. He set out with his family, and when he reached the valley of Ṭuwā, where the Mount (al-Ṭūr) is, a son was born to him on a cold, dark, snowy winter night. It was a Friday night. He had lost his way, and his flock had scattered, when he saw a fire from the side of the Mount. ﴿So he said to his family (p-24) "Wait here"﴾: remain where you are. Ḥamzah recited «لِأهْلِهِ امْكُثُوا ها هُنا» (li-ahlihi ummkuthū hā hunā), and in «al-Qaṣaṣ» (the Chapter of the Narratives) he read the hā' with a ḍammah when connected (fī al-waṣl), while the rest read it with a kasrah. ﴿Indeed I have perceived a fire﴾: I have seen it with a sight free of doubt. It is said that īnās (perceiving) means seeing what one is comforted by. ﴿Perhaps I may bring you from it a live coal﴾: a burning brand from the fire, and it is said a glowing ember. ﴿Or find at the fire some guidance﴾: a guide who will show me the way, or who will guide me to the gates of the religion, for the thoughts of the righteous incline towards this in everything that occurs to them. Since the attainment of these two was conditional, the matter concerning them was framed in terms of hope (rajā'), unlike the perceiving, which was certain; for this reason he affirmed it for them, so that they would settle their minds upon it. The sense of elevation in ﴿at the fire﴾ is that its people are overlooking it, or that they are occupying the place near it, as Sibawayh said regarding «مَرَرْتُ بِزَيْدٍ» (I passed by Zayd): that it is an adhesion to a place that is near it.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 11–12:

﴿So when he came to it﴾, i.e., the fire, he found a white fire blazing in a green tree. ﴿He was called: "O Musa!"﴾.

﴿"Indeed I am your Lord"﴾. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read it with a fath (i.e., "bi-anni"), while the rest read it with a kasra, either by implying a verb of saying (qawl) or by treating the call (nida') as if it were speech. The repetition of the pronoun is for emphasis and affirmation. It is said that when he was called, he asked: "Who is speaking?" He was told: "I am Allah." Then Iblis whispered to him: "Perhaps you are hearing the speech of a devil." So he said: "I know that it is the speech of Allah, because I hear it from all directions and with all the limbs." This is an indication that peace be upon him received His speech from his Lord through a spiritual reception (talaqqi ruhani), and then that speech took the form of his body and passed into the common sense (al-hiss al-mushtarak), and was imprinted in it without being restricted to a particular limb or direction. ﴿"So take off your sandals"﴾. He was commanded to do this because going barefoot is humility and good manners, and for this reason the early generation (al-salaf) performed circumambulation barefoot. It is said that it was because his sandals were ritually impure, as they were made of the untanned skin of a donkey. It is also said that the meaning is: empty your heart of family and wealth. ﴿"Indeed you are in the sacred valley"﴾, as a reason for the command to show reverence to the place. The word muqaddas (sacred) may bear both meanings.

﴿"Tuwa"﴾ is an explicative apposition ('atf bayan) to the valley, and Ibn 'Amir and the Kufans gave it tanwin, by interpreting it as a place. It is said that it is like "thana" (twice) from "tayy" (folding), a verbal noun (masdar) for ﴿was called﴾ or for ﴿sacred﴾, meaning: he was called twice, or it was sanctified twice.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verses 13–14:

﴿And I have chosen you﴾: I have selected you for prophethood. Hamza recited «وَإنّا اخْتَرْناكَ» (wa-inna ikhtarnaka, "and We have chosen you").

﴿So listen to what is revealed﴾: "to what is revealed" refers to what is revealed to you, or to the revelation itself. The lam (ل) may be construed with either of the two verbs.

﴿Indeed, I am Allah; there is no deity except Me, so worship Me﴾: this is a substitute (badal) for "what is revealed," indicating that it is restricted to affirming the Oneness of God (tawhid), which is the culmination of knowledge, and to the command to worship, which is the perfection of action. ﴿And establish prayer for My remembrance﴾: He singled it out for mention and gave it a separate command, for the reason to which He attached its establishment, namely, remembering the One worshipped and occupying the heart and tongue with His remembrance. It has been said that ﴿for My remembrance﴾ means because I have mentioned it in the books and commanded it; or because I will mention you with praise; or for My remembrance specifically, that you not show off in it and not mix it with the remembrance of others. It has also been said that it means for the times of My remembrance, which are the appointed times of prayer; or for the remembrance of My prayer. This is based on what is narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever sleeps through a prayer or forgets it, let him make it up when he remembers it," for Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿And establish prayer for My remembrance﴾.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (*Anwar al-Tanzil*) on surah 20, verses 15–16:

﴿Indeed, the Hour is coming﴾, certainly, without doubt. ﴿I almost conceal it﴾: I intend to conceal its time, or I am close to concealing it, so that I do not say that it is coming. Had it not been for what the reports say about its coming, which contain kindness and the removal of excuses, I would not have informed you of it. Or the meaning is ﴿I almost reveal it﴾, from *akhfāhu*, when one removes its concealment (*khafā'*). The recitation (*qira'ah*) with a *fatḥah*, *min khafāhu*, meaning "when he made it manifest," supports this. ﴿So that every soul may be recompensed for what it strives for﴾: this is related to ﴿coming﴾, or, on the last meaning, to ﴿I conceal it﴾ (p-25)

﴿I conceal it﴾ according to the last meaning.

﴿So let not one who does not believe in it turn you away from it﴾: from believing in the Hour, or from the prayer. ﴿One who does not believe in it﴾ is a prohibition addressed to the disbeliever, that he should not turn Moses, upon him be peace, away from it. The intended meaning is the prohibition of his being turned away from it, like their saying, "Let me not see you here," as an alert that his sound nature, if left to its own state, would choose it and would not turn away from it, and that he should be firm in his religion, for the turning away of the disbeliever occurs only because of weakness in that religion. ﴿And follows his desire﴾: the inclination of the self toward sensual pleasures, which are gross, so that his sight falls short of anything beyond them.

﴿Then you will perish﴾: you will be ruined by being turned away, through his turning you away.

﴿وَما تِلْكَ﴾ ("And what is that") is an interrogative that carries the sense of rousing Moses to attention toward the wonders God was about to show him in it. ﴿بِيَمِينِكَ﴾ ("in your right hand") is a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative, a grammatical state clause), referring to the sense of the demonstrative. It is also said to be a ṣila (relative complement) of ﴿تِلْكَ﴾. ﴿يا مُوسى﴾ ("O Moses") is a repetition, for the sake of increasing intimacy and attentiveness.

﴿قالَ هي عَصايَ﴾ ("He said: It is my staff"). **Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on Surah 20, verses 19–21:**

﴿He said, "Throw it down, O Moses."﴾ ﴿So he threw it down, and suddenly it was a snake, moving swiftly.﴾ It is said that when he threw it down, the staff turned into a yellow snake, as thick as the staff. Then it swelled and grew large. For this reason it was called *jann* (a small snake or serpent) at one time, looking to its origin (*al-mabda'*), and *thu'ban* (a large serpent) at another time, considering its end result (*al-muntaha*). It was also called *hayyah* (snake) at another time, using the general term that covers both states. It is also said that it was as huge as a *thu'ban* and as quick as a *jann*, and for this reason He said, "as if it were a *jann*."

﴿He said, "Take hold of it and do not fear."﴾ When he saw it as a snake that moved swiftly and swallowed stones and trees, he was frightened and fled from it. ﴿We will return it to its former state.﴾ *Sirah* here means its form and its earlier condition. It is a noun of the verb *sar* (to travel), used metaphorically for a way or a state. Its grammatical status as an accusative may be explained in one of several ways: by the removal of the preposition (*naz' al-khafid*, i.e., the omission of a preposition that would otherwise govern it); or by taking *a'ada* as transferred from *'adah* in the sense of *'ada ilayhi* ("returned to it"); or as an adverbial accusative of place (*zarf*), meaning "We will return it in its way"; or by supposing a verb to govern it, meaning "We will return the staff, after its departure, moving in its former manner, so that you benefit from it as you benefited before." It is said that when his Lord said this to him, his soul was reassured, to the point that he put his hand into its mouth and seized it by its jaws.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verses 22–24:

﴿And draw your hand to your side﴾ to your flank, beneath the upper arm. It is said that every two sides have a "janah" (wing), like the two wings of an army (ʿaskar), by metaphor from the two wings of a bird; they are named so because it inclines (yajnahuhuma) them when flying. ﴿It will come forth white﴾ as if it were radiant. ﴿Without harm﴾ without disease or ugliness; by this he refers euphemistically to leprosy (baras), just as "al-sawʾah" (the private part) is used euphemistically for the ʿawrah (the parts that must be covered), because natural dispositions shrink from it and recoil from it. ﴿As another sign﴾ a second miracle. It is either a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun in ﴿It will come forth white﴾, or from its pronoun, or an object (mafʿūl) with an implied verb, such as "take" or "dūnaka" (take it for yourself).

﴿That We may show you of Our greater signs﴾ this is connected to the implied verb mentioned, or to what is indicated by "sign," or to the story by which We gave proof, or "We did that so that We may show you." ﴿Greater﴾ (al-kubrā) is an adjective of "Our signs," or the object of "We may show you," and ﴿of Our signs﴾ is a circumstantial clause from it.

﴿Go to Pharaoh﴾ with these two signs, and call him to worship. ﴿Indeed, he has transgressed﴾ he disobeyed and became arrogant.

﴿He said, "My Lord, expand my breast for me"﴾ ﴿and ease my task for me﴾. When God commanded him with a great undertaking and a weighty matter, he asked Him to expand his chest and open up his heart, so that he could bear its burdens, endure its hardships, and receive what would be revealed to him. There was a speech impediment (*rattah*, a defect in pronunciation) in his tongue, caused by a live coal he had put into his mouth. This happened because Pharaoh once carried him and took hold of his beard and plucked it. Pharaoh became angry and ordered him killed, but Asiya said, "He is a child who cannot distinguish between a live coal and a ruby." Those who hold that it was removed rely on His words, ﴿You have been granted your request, O Moses﴾. Those who do not say so argue from His words, ﴿He is more eloquent in speech than I﴾ and His words, ﴿and he can hardly express himself clearly﴾. Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verses 29–32:

﴿And appoint for me a minister from my family﴾ ﴿Harun, my brother﴾, who will assist me in what You have charged me with. The derivation of wazir (minister) is either from wizr (burden), because he bears the weight on behalf of his amir (leader), or from wazar, which means refuge, because the amir seeks protection in his opinion and takes refuge in him in his affairs; from this comes muwazarah (support). It is also said that its origin is azir, from al-azr meaning strength, with the form fa'il in the sense of mufa'il, like 'ashir (companion) and jalis (companion), and its hamzah was changed to waw, as it was changed in muwazir.

The two objects of ijʻal (appoint) are (wazir) and (Harun). He placed the second of them first for the sake of giving it importance. (Li) (for me) may be a complement, or a circumstantial phrase, or (li wazir) (for me, a minister) with (Harun) as an explanatory apposition to (wazir), or (wazir min ahli) (a minister from my family) with (li) serving as an explanation, like His saying ﴿and there is none comparable to Him, anyone﴾. (Akhi) (my brother) in all these cases is either a substitute (badal) for (Harun) or a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is implied.

﴿Strengthen my back through him﴾ ﴿and make him share in my task﴾, in the imperative form. Ibn 'Amir recited both in the form of the indicative, considering them as answers to the imperative.

It is also said that its origin is azir, from al-azr meaning strength, with the form fa'il in the sense of mufa'il, like 'ashir (companion) and jalis (companion), and its hamzah was changed to waw, as it was changed in muwazir.

The two objects of ijʻal (appoint) are (wazir) and (Harun). He placed the second of them first for the sake of giving it importance. (Li) (for me) may be a complement, or a circumstantial phrase, or (li wazir) (for me, a minister) with (Harun) as an explanatory apposition to (wazir), or (wazir min ahli) (a minister from my family) with (li) serving as an explanation, like His saying ﴿and there is none comparable to Him, anyone﴾. (Akhi) (my brother) in all these cases is either a substitute (badal) for (Harun) or a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is implied.

﴿Strengthen my back through him﴾ ﴿and make him share in my task﴾, in the imperative form. Ibn 'Amir recited both in the form of the indicative, considering them as answers to the imperative.

﴿That we may glorify You much﴾ ﴿and remember You much﴾. Indeed, cooperation stirs up desires and leads to the multiplication and increase of good.

﴿Indeed You were ever Seeing of us﴾, knowing our conditions, and that cooperation is among the things that set us right, and that Harun is an excellent helper to me in what You commanded me to do. (p-27)

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verses 36–38:

﴿He said: "You have been given your request, O Moses."﴾ That is, your request (mas'ul), where fu'l is used in the sense of maf'ul, as in khubz (bread) and akl (food) meaning the baked (makhbuz) and the eaten (ma'kul).

﴿And We had already bestowed favour upon you another time﴾ That is, We bestowed Our blessing upon you at another time.

﴿When We inspired (awhayna) to your mother﴾ by inspiration (ilham), or in a dream, or through the tongue of a prophet of her time, or an angel; not in the manner of prophethood, just as inspiration was given to Maryam (Mary). ﴿That which is inspired﴾ means that which can only be known through revelation (wahy), or that which should be inspired and is not neglected, due to its great importance and the extreme care given to it.

﴿That throw him into the chest﴾: meaning "[it is] with (bi-anna) 'throw him,'" or "[an explanatory] ay 'throw him,'" because revelation (al-waḥy, here meaning inspired communication) carries the sense of speech.

﴿Then let him be thrown into the river﴾. The verb qadhf is used both for casting and for placing, as in His saying, ﴿And He cast terror into their hearts﴾, and likewise ramy (throwing), as in the verse: "A youth whom God cast with beauty while still growing up."

﴿Let the river cast him onto the shore﴾. Since the river's casting him onto the shore was a matter bound to occur, because the will is tied to it, [the verse] treats the sea as if it were a discerning being obeying His command, and it puts the response in the form of a command. It is preferable that all the pronouns be taken as referring to Moses, for the sake of the wording. So the one cast into the river and the one thrown onto the shore is, in essence, the chest, but in its accidental relation it is Moses.

﴿An enemy to Me and an enemy to him will take him﴾ is the response to ﴿let him be cast﴾. The repetition of ﴿enemy﴾ is for emphasis, or because the first refers to what actually is and the second to what is expected. It is said that she (his mother) put cotton inside the chest, placed him in it, then sealed it with pitch and threw it into the river. A stream ran from it to the garden of Pharaoh, and the water carried it to him and brought it to a pool in the garden. Pharaoh was sitting at its edge with his wife Asiya bint Muzahim. He ordered that it be taken out and opened, and there was a child, the most beautiful of people in face. So he loved him with an intense love, as He, glory be to Him, said:

﴿And I cast upon you love from Me﴾, that is, a love originating from Me, which I had planted in hearts such that whoever sees you can hardly bear to be apart from you. For this reason Pharaoh loved you. It is also permissible for (min-nī) to be connected to (alqaytu), meaning "I made you beloved," and whoever God loves, hearts love. The apparent meaning of the wording is that the sea cast him onto its shore, which is its bank, because the water dragged him there and so he was picked up from it. However, it is not far-fetched to interpret the shore as the side of the mouth of its river.

﴿And that you be reared under My eye﴾: to be nurtured and treated well, while I am your guardian and watcher. The conjunction is upon an implied cause, like "so that he would show kindness to you," or upon the preceding clause with an implied verb of cause, like "I did that." It is also read as (wa-litusna'a) with the vowel of the lam being kasra and with sukūn, and with jazm, understood as a command. And (wa-litasna'a) with naṣb and a fatḥa on the tā', meaning "and that your work might be under My eye, so that you would not disobey My command in it."

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 40:

﴿When your sister walked﴾ is an adverbial complement (*zarf*) modifying either (*alqaytu*) "I cast" or (*litusna'a*) "so that you might be raised," or it is a substitute (*badal*) for ﴿when We revealed﴾, on the understanding that the intended time is an extended period. ﴿Then she said: "Shall I direct you to someone who will take charge of him?"﴾ This is because he would not accept the breasts of wet-nurses. So his sister Maryam came, seeking out news of him, and found them looking for a wet-nurse whose breast he would accept. So she said, ﴿Shall I direct you?﴾ and she brought his mother, and he accepted her breast. ﴿So We returned you to your mother﴾ in fulfilment of Our words, ﴿Indeed, We will return him to you﴾, ﴿that her eye might be comforted﴾ by your meeting. ﴿And that she might not grieve﴾, either she over your separation, or you over your separation from her and the loss of her compassion. ﴿And you killed a soul﴾, namely the soul of the Copt whom the Israelite sought help against. ﴿And We delivered you from distress﴾, the distress of having killed him, out of fear of the punishment of God the Exalted, and of Pharaoh's retaliation, by way of forgiveness and safety from him through emigration to Madyan. ﴿And We tested you with a testing﴾, that is, We put you to trial with a trial, or with various kinds of trial. This reading takes *futun* as a plural of *fatan* or *fitnah*, with the feminine ending disregarded, as in the plurals *hujūz* and *budūr* from *hujzah* and *badrah*. ﴿So We delivered you time after time.﴾ This is a summary of what he endured on his journey: emigration from his homeland, separation from his companions, walking on foot in fear, the lack of provisions, hiring himself out, and other things, the first of which is what has been mentioned above. ﴿Then you stayed for years among the people of Madyan.﴾ You remained among them for ten years, fulfilling the better of the two terms. Madyan lies eight stages from Egypt. ﴿Then you came at an appointed time﴾ that I had decreed, so that I might speak with you and make you a prophet, neither ahead of its appointed time nor behind it; or at a measure of age at which revelation is sent down to the prophets. ﴿O Musa!﴾ He repeated the name after what is the goal of the narration, to draw attention to that.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verses 41–42:

﴿And I have chosen you for Myself﴾ — and I have selected you for My love, like one whom the King has brought near and singled out for Himself, bestowing on him honour of that kind.

﴿Go, you and your brother, with My signs﴾ — with My miracles. ﴿And do not slacken﴾ — do not grow weary, nor fall short. It is also read as ﴿tanniyā﴾ with a kasra on the tā' (tinniyā).

﴿in remembrance of Me﴾ — do not forget Me wherever you turn. It has also been said: in conveying My remembrance and calling (people) to Me.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 43–44:

﴿Go, both of you, to Pharaoh; indeed he has transgressed.﴾ Musa, upon him be peace, was first commanded with this alone, and here he is commanded with him and his brother, so there is no repetition (takrir).

It was said that He revealed to Harun that he should go out to meet Musa, and it was said that he heard of his approach and went to meet him.

﴿So speak to him gently speech﴾ like ﴿Would you like to purify yourself, and that I guide you to your Lord so that you fear Him?﴾ For this is an invitation in the form of an offer and a counsel, out of caution lest his foolishness lead him to attack you both, or out of respect for what he has of the right of upbringing over you. It was said that they addressed him by a kunya, and he had three kunyas: Abu al-Abbas, Abu al-Walid, and Abu Murrah. It was said that He granted him a youth that would not age after it and a kingship that would not end except by death. ﴿Perhaps he will be mindful or fear﴾ is connected to "go" (idhhaba) or to "speak" (qula), meaning: undertake the matter in hope and in the expectation that your effort will bear fruit and not be in vain, for the one who hopes is diligent and the one who despairs is making a pretence. The benefit of sending them and of exerting them in striving, while He knows that he will not believe, is the establishment of the proof, the cutting off of excuses, and the manifestation, among the course of that, of the signs that occurred; and [the benefit is] mindfulness for the one who is certain and fear for the one who imagines [the danger]. For this reason He put the first first, that is: if he does not become certain of your truthfulness and is not mindful, then he will at least imagine it and so fear.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verses 45–46:

﴿They said, "Our Lord, indeed we fear that he will hasten against us [with punishment] or that he will transgress."﴾ That is, that he will hasten against us with punishment and not be patient until the completion of the call and the manifestation of the miracle. From "faraṭa" (to precede), as in "al-fārit" (one who goes ahead), and a horse called "faras faraṭ" which outstrips the horses. It has also been read "yafruṭa" (with a damma on the ya and the ra' vowelled as a transitive form) from "afraṭtahu," meaning you urged him toward haste; that is, we fear that some driver of his, whether from arrogance, fear for his kingdom, a human devil or a jinn devil, will drive him to hasten the punishment. And "yafruṭa" may also be from "al-ifrāṭ" (excess) in harming.

﴿Or that he will transgress.﴾ That is, or that he will increase in transgression, going beyond bounds so that he says about you what is not fitting, due to his audacity, harshness, and freedom from good manners.

﴿He said, "Do not fear; indeed I am with you﴾ by protection and support. ﴿I hear and I see.﴾ I hear what passes between you and him of speech and action, so I bring about in every matter that turns his evil away from you and necessitates My support for you. It is also possible that the meaning of "I am with you" is that I am your guardian, hearing and seeing; and a guardian who is capable, hearing and seeing, completes the protection.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verses 47–48:

﴿So go to him and say: "We are both messengers of your Lord, so send the Children of Israel with us"﴾, meaning release them. ﴿And do not torment them﴾ with harsh burdens and the killing of their young sons. They were in the hands of the Qibt (Copts), who made them serve and wearied them with labour, and they would kill their male children in some years but not in others. The fact that the coming is followed by this request indicates that rescuing the believers from the disbelievers is more important than calling them to faith. It is also possible that it is meant as a gradual approach in the call.

﴿We have certainly come to you with a sign from your Lord﴾ is a sentence confirming what the preceding speech contained of the claim to messengership. He used the singular "sign," although he had two signs, because the purpose is to establish the claim with its proof, not to indicate the unity or multiplicity of the evidence. Similarly are His words: ﴿We have certainly come to you with a clear proof﴾, ﴿So bring a sign﴾, and ﴿He said: "Even if I brought you something manifest?"﴾.

﴿And peace upon those who follow the guidance﴾: the peace of the angels and the keepers of Paradise upon the rightly guided, or safety in both abodes for them.

﴿Indeed, it has been revealed to us that the punishment is upon him who denies and turns away﴾: that the punishment of both abodes is upon those who deny the messengers. Perhaps the change of structure, the explicit statement of the threat, and its emphasis are because warning at the beginning of the matter is more important, more effective, and better suited to the reality.

He said, "Who, then, is your Lord, O Musa?" This is said after the two of them had come to him and said what they had been commanded to say. The question is omitted, probably because the situation indicates it, since the obedient person, when commanded to do something, certainly does it. He addressed the two of them but singled out Musa, peace be upon him, with the call because he is the principal, and Harun is his vizier (wazir) and follower. Or it is because he knew that Musa had a speech impediment (ratta) and his brother had eloquence, so he wanted to silence him (yufhimahu). This is indicated by his saying: ﴿Am I not better than this one who is despised and can hardly express himself?﴾

He said, "Our Lord is the One who gave everything ﴿its creation﴾" among the kinds, ﴿khalqahu﴾, meaning its form and shape that corresponds to its possible perfection. Or it means He gave His creatures everything they need and by which they benefit. He put the second object (al-maf'ul al-thani, the second object of the verb) first because it is what is intended to be explained. It is said that He gave every animal its counterpart in creation and form, a mate. It is also read as ﴿khalaqahu﴾, as an attribute (sifah) of the added-to or the adding noun, which is an irregular reading, and then the second object is omitted, meaning: He gave every created thing what sets it right. ﴿Then guided﴾: then He made it know how to benefit from what it was given and how to reach, through it, its survival and perfection, either by choice or by nature. This is an answer of the utmost eloquence (balaghah) in its brevity, and in its expressing the existence of all beings in their entire ranks. Its indication is that the One who is self-sufficient, who has power in Himself, who bestows favor absolutely, is God, exalted is He, and that everything other than Him is in need of Him and is a recipient of His favor in its essence, its attributes and its actions. For this reason the one who disbelieved was struck dumb and silenced from entering into argument with Him, so he saw no course but to turn the discourse away from it.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 51–52:

﴿He said, "Then what is the state of the former generations?"﴾ That is, what is their condition after their death, in terms of happiness and misery.

﴿He said, "Its knowledge is with my Lord"﴾ That is, it is an unseen matter that none knows except Him, and I am merely a servant like you; I know nothing of it except what He has informed me.

﴿in a Book﴾ Recorded in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz). It is also permissible that this be a figurative expression for the firmness of His knowledge, of what He has entrusted to the world and restricted to the scribes, and this is supported by it. ﴿My Lord neither errs nor forgets.﴾ Error (dalal) is that you mistake a thing in its place so that you do not find it; forgetting (nisyan) is that you lose it to the point that it does not occur to your mind. Both are impossible for the One who knows by His essence. It is also permissible that his question was an objection concerning the comprehensiveness of God Most High's power over all things and His distinguishing some of them with various forms and properties, since that requires His knowledge of the details and particulars of things. How, with the great number of the past generations, the length of their periods, and the distance of their regions, did His knowledge encompass them (p-30)

and their parts and their conditions? So the meaning of the answer is: His knowledge, may He be exalted, encompasses all of that, and it is recorded with Him; He neither errs nor forgets.

﴿And He threaded for you therein roads﴾: and He made for you therein roads between the mountains, the valleys and the deserts, which you travel from land to land, so that you may reach their benefits.

﴿And sent down from the sky water﴾: rain.

﴿Then We brought forth thereby﴾: He shifted from the third person (ghaybah) to the first person (takallum) in narrating the speech of God Most High, to draw attention to the manifestation within it of evidence for perfect power and wisdom, and to announce that He is obeyed, such that diverse things submit to His will. It is the plural of shatit, like marid and marda, meaning scattered (mutafarriqat) in forms, purposes and benefits, some of which are suitable for people and some for animals. Therefore He said:

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verses 54–55:

﴿Eat and graze your livestock﴾. This is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring back to the pronoun in ﴿And We brought forth﴾, on the understanding of an implied saying: that is, "We brought forth various kinds of plants, saying: 'Eat and graze.'" The meaning is that they were made ready for your benefit, for eating and fodder, with permission granted for their use. ﴿Indeed, in that are signs for people of intellect﴾, that is, for those of sound minds that restrain (nahy) from following falsehood and from committing abominations. Nuha is the plural of nahyah (restraint, intellect).

﴿From it We created you﴾, for the earth is the origin of the creation of your first father and the first material of your bodies. ﴿And into it We return you﴾ by death and the dissolution of the parts. ﴿And from it We bring you forth once more﴾ by reassembling your scattered parts, which have become mixed with the dust, into their former forms and returning the spirits to them.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verses 56–57:

﴿And We certainly showed him Our signs﴾: We made him see them, or We made him know their soundness (ṣiḥḥatahā). ﴿All of them﴾: an emphasis, indicating the comprehensiveness either of the kinds (of signs) or of the individual instances. Alternatively, the intended meaning of "Our signs" is the known signs, namely the nine signs specific to Musa (Moses). Or it means that he (peace be upon him) showed him his signs and enumerated for him the miracles that others had been given. ﴿But he denied﴾: Musa, out of extreme obstinacy on his part. ﴿and refused﴾: to accept faith and obedience, due to his arrogance (ʿutuwwihi).

﴿He said: "Have you come to us to drive us out of our land﴾: the land of Egypt. ﴿with your magic, O Musa?﴾ This is an excuse and bewilderment, and a proof that he knew that he (Musa) was in the right, to the point that he feared him for his kingdom, for a sorcerer cannot cause a king like him to be driven out of his land.

Or it is a substitute (badal, apposition) for ﴿مَوْعِدًا﴾, on the assumption of an implied noun "place" (makān) as its genitive complement. ﴿So Pharaoh withdrew and gathered his scheming﴾: that is, what is used for plotting, meaning the magicians and their instruments. ﴿Then he came﴾ to the appointed place.

﴿Moses said to them: "Woe to you! Do not fabricate against Allah a lie, [by calling] His signs magic, lest He destroy you with a punishment"﴾: that is, He will ruin you and uproot you. It is recited with the vowel on the yā' (yusḥita, with ḍamma) by Ḥamzah, al-Kisā'ī, Ḥafṣ and Ya‘qūb, from al-ISḥāt (ilsaḥat, "to destroy utterly"), which is the dialect of Najd and Tamīm, whereas al-suḥt (al-suḥt, "destruction") is the dialect of the Ḥijāz. ﴿And he has indeed failed who fabricates﴾: just as Pharaoh failed, for he fabricated and schemed so that kingship might remain with him, but it did not benefit him.

It has also been said that the original was إنَّهُ هَذانِ لَهُما ساحِرانِ (innahu hadhani lahuma sahiran, "indeed, these two, for them are magicians"), so the pronoun was omitted; but the objection is that what is emphasized with the lam does not properly admit omission. ﴿So gather your plot﴾: resolve upon it (fa-azmiʿūhu), and make it a unified plan agreed upon, such that not one of you holds back from it. Abu ʿAmr (Abu ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlaʾ) read ﴿fa-ajmiʿū﴾, and his reading is supported by the statement ﴿then he gathered his plot﴾. ﴿Then come in a row﴾: lined up, for that is more awe-inspiring in the hearts of those who see. It is said they were seventy thousand, each with a rope and a staff, and they advanced upon him in a single advance. ﴿And he who prevails today is indeed successful﴾: whoever overcomes attains what he seeks; and this is a parenthetical interjection (iʿtiraḍ).

The clause introduced by ﴿an﴾ (that) with what follows it is either in the accusative, governed by a hidden verb, or in the nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject (khabar), meaning: choose your throwing first, or our throwing, or the matter is your throwing or our throwing.

﴿He said, "Rather, you throw."﴾ This was a reciprocal courtesy, matching their courtesy with courtesy, and a sign of indifference to their magic. It also accommodated what they had suggested, namely their inclination to begin by mentioning the first item (the rods) in their own favour, and it changed the arrangement of the speech into a more eloquent form. It was also so that they would bring forth what they had and exhaust their utmost effort, and then God would manifest His authority: He would hurl the truth against falsehood, and it would crush it.

﴿Then, behold, their ropes and their staffs seemed to him, by their magic, to be moving.﴾ That is: they threw, and behold, their ropes and their staffs. The "fa-idha" (إذا, "then suddenly") is for sudden surprise. The verification is that it is also a temporal particle (ظرفية, adverbial of time), which requires a verb that governs it (متعلق) and a clause that is added to it. However, it is specifically restricted so that the governing element is the verb of suddenness (فعل المفاجأة, a verb indicating the sudden occurrence), and the clause that follows is a nominal clause (ابتدائية, beginning with a noun). The meaning is: they threw, and so Musa, peace be upon him, was startled at the time the ropes and staffs were made to appear to be moving through their magic. This was because they had smeared them with mercury, and when the sun shone upon them, they began to move, so it appeared to him that they were moving.

Ibn 'Amir, according to the transmission of Ibn Dhakwan and Ruh, read "takhayyala" (تَخَيَّلَ) with a ta', attributing it to the pronoun of the ropes and staffs, and making "annahā tas'ā" (أنَّها تَسْعى) a substitution from it, a badal al-ishtimal (بدل الاشتمال, a substitute that includes the thing substituted for). It was also read as "yukhayyilu" (يُخَيِّلُ) with a ya', attributing it to God, Exalted is He, and "takhayyala" was read with the meaning "tatakhayyalu" (تَتَخَيَّلُ, "they appear to be moving").

﴿So Moses felt a fear within himself.﴾ He concealed within himself a fear of being taken by surprise, as human nature requires, or a fear that people might be seized by doubt and so not follow him.

﴿We said, "Do not fear,"﴾ what you imagined. ﴿Indeed, you are the superior one.﴾ This is a justification for the prohibition and an affirmation of his triumph, emphasized by being a resumptive sentence (istiʾnaf, a new sentence that begins without grammatical connection to what precedes it), the particle of confirmation (ḥarf al-taḥqīq), the repetition of the pronoun, the definiteness of the predicate, the word "superior," which indicates manifest dominance, and the comparative form.

﴿And throw what is in your right hand.﴾ He left it indefinite and did not say "your staff," either to belittle it, meaning: do not mind the abundance of their ropes and staves, and throw the small stick that is in your hand; or to magnify it, meaning: do not be impressed by the multitude of these objects, and regard it as great, for what is in your right hand is greater in effect than them, so throw it. ﴿It will swallow what they have crafted.﴾ It swallows it by the power of God Most High. Its original form is tatalaqqafu, so one of the two tāʾs was elided. The tāʾ of the present tense may be feminine, or it may be a second-person address, by attributing the verb to its cause. Ibn ʿĀmir, in the transmission of Ibn Dhakwān, read it with ḍamma (rafʿ), as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) or a resumptive sentence. Ḥafṣ read it with jazm and lightening, taking it as from laqiftuhu in the sense of talaqqaftuhu.

﴿What they have made is only﴾ that what they forged and fabricated.

﴿A sorcerer's trick.﴾ It was also read in the accusative, on the basis that the particle ma is a preventive particle (kāffa) and that kayd is the object of ṣanaʿū. Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī read siḥrin, meaning "one possessing magic," or naming the sorcerer as magic for emphasis, or attaching the trick to magic in an explanatory genitive, as in the phrase ʿilm fiqh ("knowledge of jurisprudence"). He used the singular "sorcerer" because the intended meaning is the generic type, which is why He said: ﴿and the sorcerer does not succeed,﴾ meaning this category. The indefiniteness of the first noun matches the indefiniteness of the noun it is attached to, as in the verse of al-ʿAjjāj:

"On the day when souls see what they have prepared
in the striving of a worldly life that has long been extended."

It is as if it were said: "What they made is a magical trick."

﴿Wherever he comes.﴾ Wherever he was, and wherever he arrived.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 70:

﴿So the magicians were thrown down prostrate﴾ That is, he threw (his staff), and it swallowed them up. Thus it became clear to the magicians that it was not magic, but rather a sign from the signs of God and one of His miracles. So that, which they saw, cast them upon their faces in prostration to God, in repentance for what they had done, in seeking His pardon, and in glorifying what they had seen. ﴿They said: We believe in the Lord of Aaron and Moses﴾ Aaron is mentioned first because of his old age, or for the sake of the rhyme of the verse, or because Pharaoh raised Moses in his childhood; so had he mentioned only Moses, or mentioned him first, it might have been supposed that the intended meaning was Pharaoh, and the mention of Aaron serves to make clear that he is a follower (of Moses). It is related that they saw in their prostration the Garden and their dwelling places in it.

﴿He said: "Have you believed in him before I gave you permission?"﴾ That is, in Musa (Moses). The *lām* (ﻝ) in ﴿لَهُ﴾ is used because the verb includes the meaning of following (*ittiba'*).

Qunbul and Hafs read ﴿آمَنتُمْ لَهُ﴾ as a statement (*khabar*), while the rest read it as a question (*istifham*).

﴿before I gave you permission﴾ to believe in him.

﴿Indeed, he is your chief﴾, meaning your great one in your craft and the most knowledgeable of you in it, or your master (*ustadh*).

﴿who taught you magic﴾, and you had colluded over what you did.

﴿I will surely cut off your hands and your feet on opposite sides﴾: the right hand and the left foot. The *min* (مِن) in ﴿مِن خِلافٍ﴾ is inceptive (*ibtida'iyyah*), as if the cutting began from one limb opposing another. It and its genitive complement occupy the position of the accusative (*ḥayyiz al-naṣb*) as a circumstantial state (*ḥāl*), meaning: I will cut them off while they are differing (in side). It is also read ﴿لَأقْطَعَنَّ﴾ and ﴿وَلَأصْلِبَنَّ﴾ with the lighter pronunciation (*takhfif*).

﴿And I will surely crucify you upon the trunks of palm trees﴾. He likened the crucified person's being fixed to the trunk with the containment of the contained within the container. He was the first to crucify.

﴿And you will surely know which of us﴾ he means himself and Musa, because of his saying ﴿you believed in him﴾. The *lām* with belief in the Book of God is for other than God. He intended by this to belittle Musa and mock him, for he had no part in punishment. It was said: the Lord of Musa, in whom they believed.

﴿is more severe in punishment and more lasting﴾, that is, more enduring in punishment.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 72:

﴿They said: "We will not prefer you﴾ (lan nu'thiraka) over ﴿what has come to us﴾ — i.e., lan nukhtarака, "we will not choose you" — ﴿of the clear proofs﴾ that Musa brought, and it is permissible that the pronoun in it (bihi, "with it") refers to ma (what). ﴿From the clear signs﴾ — the evident miracles. ﴿And Him who created us﴾ is either a conjunction with ﴿what has come to us﴾, or it is an oath. ﴿So decree what you will decree﴾ — "what you are a decreer of," i.e., one who makes it (sani'uhu), or one who rules by it (hakim bihi). ﴿You only decree regarding this worldly life﴾ — you only do what you desire, or you rule by what you see in this world. ﴿But the Hereafter is better and more lasting﴾ — this serves as a justification for what precedes it and a preparation for what follows. It was also read as "tuqda hadhihi al-hayatu al-dunya" (passive), like your saying: "ṣīma yawmu al-Jumu'ah" (the day of Friday was fasted).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 73:

﴿Indeed, we have believed in our Lord, that He may forgive us our sins﴾ of disbelief and disobedience. ﴿And [forgive us] the sorcery to which you compelled us﴾ of opposing the miracle. It is narrated that they said to Pharaoh, "Show us Moses asleep," and they found that his staff was guarding him. So they said, "This is not sorcery, for when a sorcerer sleeps, his sorcery becomes void," but he refused except that they should oppose him. ﴿And Allah is better and more enduring﴾ in reward, or better in recompense and more enduring in punishment.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verses 74–76:

﴿Indeed﴾: indeed, the matter (al-amr). ﴿Whoever comes to his Lord as a criminal﴾: by dying in his disbelief and disobedience. ﴿For him is Hell; he will neither die therein﴾ so that he might find rest, ﴿nor live﴾ a comfortable life.

﴿And whoever comes to Him as a believer, having done righteous deeds﴾ in this world. ﴿For those are the high ranks﴾: the lofty abodes.

﴿Gardens of perpetual residence﴾ is a substitute (badal) for "the ranks." ﴿Beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal), and the element governing it is the meaning of the demonstrative (al-ishara) or of settling (al-istiqrar). ﴿And that is the recompense of one who purifies himself﴾: who purifies himself from the impurities of disbelief and sins. The three verses may be from the speech of the sorcerers, or they may be the beginning of a speech from God, the Exalted.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 77:

﴿And We certainly revealed to Musa: "Travel by night with My servants."﴾ That is, from Egypt. ﴿So strike for them a dry path﴾ i.e., make for them (a path), from the expression "ḍaraba lahu fī mālihi sahman" (he set aside for him a share in his wealth), or from "ittakhadha min ḍarb al-labin" (he made it from the striking of bricks) when he shaped it. ﴿through the sea, dry﴾ (yabasan): "yābis" (dry), a verbal noun (maṣdar) used as an adjective. It is said "yabisa yabasan wa yubsan," like "saqima saqaman wa suqman" (to be sick), and for this reason it is used as a description of the feminine, so it is said "shāh yabas" (a ewe whose milk has dried up). It has also been read "yabsan," and this is either a lightened form of it, or an adjective on the pattern of "ṣa'b," or a plural of "yābis," like "ṣaḥb," used as a description of the singular for emphasis, as in his saying:

"As if the saddle-frames of my riding-camel, when they were pressed together, were milking-vessels, ghurzan (with wooden pegs), and with me hungry (ones)."

Or it is because of its plurality in meaning, for he made for each tribe among them a path. ﴿Do not fear being overtaken﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the one commanded, i.e., secure from the enemy overtaking you; or it is a second attribute, with the returning pronoun omitted. Ḥamzah read "lā takhaf" (do not fear), taking it as a response to the imperative. ﴿and do not dread﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'nāf), i.e., "and you do not dread"; or it is conjoined to what precedes it, and the alif in it is for pausal lengthening (iṭlāq), as in His saying: ﴿and you assume about Allah assumptions﴾; or it is a circumstantial clause with the waw, and the meaning is "and do not dread the drowning."

﴿So Pharaoh followed them with his hosts.﴾ This is because Moses, peace be upon him, set out with them at the beginning of the night, and Pharaoh was informed of this and traced their trail. The meaning is: Pharaoh followed them himself, and with him his hosts, so the second object was omitted (al-maf'ul al-thani). It is also said that "fa-atba'ahum" means "fa-ittaba'ahum" (he followed them), and the reading with it supports this. The bāʾ (ba, here in "bi-junudihi") is for transitivity (al-ta'diya). It is also said that the bāʾ is redundant (mazidah), and the meaning is: his hosts followed them, and he drove them from behind.

﴿Then the sea covered them with what covered them.﴾ The pronoun refers to his hosts, the first part of it and "them." There is exaggeration and conciseness in it, meaning: there covered them what you have heard of its story, and no one knows its reality except God. It has been read "fa-ghashshahum ma ghashshahum" (with the verb in the intensive form), meaning: he covered them with what covered them. The agent is God Most High, or "what covered them," or Pharaoh, because he is the one who led them into destruction.

﴿And Pharaoh led his people astray and did not guide them.﴾ That is, he misled them in religion and did not guide them. This is said in mockery of him in His words: ﴿And I do not show you except the path of right guidance.﴾ Or it means he led them astray in the sea and they were not saved.

﴿O Children of Israel﴾ is an address to them after their deliverance from the sea and the destruction of Pharaoh, with "We said" understood before it. Alternatively, it is addressed to those among them in the time of the Prophet, peace be upon him, concerning what was done to their forefathers.

﴿Indeed We delivered you from your enemy﴾, namely Pharaoh and his people. ﴿And We appointed for you the right side of the Mount﴾ for the secret conversation of Musa (Moses) and the sending down of the Tawrah (Torah) to him. The appointment is attributed to them, though it was first Musa's and that of the seventy chosen men, because they were associated with it. ﴿And We sent down to you the manna and the quail﴾, meaning during al-tih (the wandering in the wilderness). ﴿Eat of the good things that We have provided for you﴾: its delicacies, or its lawful things.

Hamzah and al-Kisa'i (the Qur'an reciters) read «أنْجَيْتُكم» (anjaytukum), «وَواعَدْتُكم» (wa-wa'adtukum) and «ما رَزَقْتُكم» (ma razaqtukum) with the first person singular «تاء» (ta'). It is also read «وَوَعَدْتُكم» (wa-wa'adtukum) and «وَوَعَدْناكم» (wa-wa'adnakum). The word ﴿الأيْمَنَ﴾ (al-ayman, "the right") is read in the genitive case (bi-l-jarr) by adjacency (al-jiwar), like the phrase «جُحْرُ ضَبٍّ خَرِبٍ» (juhru dabbin kharibin, "the hole of a lizard that is ruined"), where «خَرِبٍ» (kharibin) is genitive because it is adjacent to «ضَبٍّ» (dabbin), though grammatically it describes «جُحْرُ» (juhr).

﴿And do not transgress therein﴾: in what We have provided you, by failing to give thanks for it, and by exceeding what God has set as limits for you concerning it, such as extravagance, insolence, and withholding from those who deserve it. ﴿Then My wrath will descend upon you﴾: then My punishment will become binding upon you, and it will be due from you, as a debt becomes due (ḥalla al-dayn) when its payment is required. ﴿And whoever incurs My wrath, he has indeed perished﴾: he has indeed fallen and been destroyed. It is also said that he has fallen into the Abyss (al-Hawiyah). Al-Kisa'i read «يَحُلُّ» (yaḥull) and «يَحْلُلْ» (yaḥlul) with a «ضَمّ» (ḍamm, vowel u), from «حَلَّ يَحُلُّ» (ḥalla yaḥullu), meaning to descend, when it descends.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verses 83–84:

﴿And what has hastened you away from your people, O Musa?﴾ This is a question about the cause of the haste, which implies its disapproval, in that haste is in itself a deficiency. Added to it is neglecting the people and giving the impression of self-exaltation over them. Therefore Musa answered both matters, and he placed the answer to the disapproval first, because it is more important.

﴿He said﴾ Musa. ﴿They are right behind me on my track﴾ That is, I did not go ahead of them except by small steps that are not customarily considered significant, and there was between me and them only a short distance by which a travelling company precede one another.

﴿And I hastened to You, my Lord, that You might be pleased﴾ For hastening to carry out Your command and to fulfil Your covenant brings about Your good pleasure.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (*Anwar al-Tanzil*) on surah 20, verses 85–86:

﴿He said, "Indeed, We have tested your people after you."﴾ We put them to trial with the worship of the calf after your departure from among them. They are those whom he left behind with Harun, and they numbered six hundred thousand. Of them, only twelve thousand were spared from worshipping the calf. ﴿And as-Samiri led them astray.﴾ By making the calf and calling them to worship it. It is recited as «wa-aḍallahum» (qira'a, a variant recitation), meaning "and the most misguided of them," because he was astray and a misleader. And it is reported that they remained upon the religion for twenty nights after his departure, and they reckoned them as forty days with their nights, and said, "We have completed the term." Then the matter of the calf occurred. This address was made to him at the time of his arrival, since nothing in the verse indicates it. It was a report from God to him about what was awaited, in the wording of what has occurred, according to His custom, for the origin of an event's occurrence is that it is in His knowledge and in accordance with His will. As-Samiri is ascribed to a tribe of the Children of Israel called as-Samirah. It is said he was a non-Arab (ʿilj) from Kirman. It is said he was from the people of Bajarma, and his name was Musa ibn Zafar, and he was a hypocrite.

﴿So Musa returned to his people﴾ after he had completed the forty days and taken the Tawrat (Torah), ﴿angry﴾ with them, ﴿grieved﴾ (asif), sorrowful over what they had done. ﴿He said, "O my people, did your Lord not promise you a good promise?"﴾ And that He would give you the Torah, in which there is guidance and light. ﴿Has the term seemed long to you?﴾ i.e., has the time, meaning the time of his separation from them, seemed long? ﴿Or do you desire that wrath from your Lord should descend upon you?﴾ i.e., should become obligatory upon you. ﴿…﴾ (p-36)

by worshipping what is a proverb of foolishness. ﴿So you broke your promise to me﴾ your pledge to me to remain steadfast in faith in God and to uphold what I commanded you. It is also said that it is from "akhlaftu wa'dahu" (I found his promise broken), i.e., you found a breach in my promise to you of returning after forty days. This does not fit the ordering by the disjunction (tardid), nor the part that follows it, nor their answer to it.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verses 87–89:

﴿They said: "We did not break our promise to you of our own power"﴾, meaning: by our having power over our own affairs, since if we had been left to ourselves and our own will, and al-Samiri had not tempted us, we would not have broken it. Nafi' and 'Asim read ﴿بِمَلْكِنا﴾ with a fatha (*bi-malkina*), and Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it with a damma (*bi-mulkina*). All three forms are, originally, dialectal variants of the verbal noun of *malaktu al-shay'* (I possessed the thing).

﴿"But we were made to carry burdens of the ornaments of the people"﴾: we carried loads of the jewelry of the Copts, which we had borrowed from them when we resolved to leave Egypt under the pretext of a wedding. It was also said that they had borrowed it for a festival they had, and then did not return it when they departed, for fear that they would find out about it. It was also said that it was what the sea had cast onto the shore after their drowning, and they took it. Perhaps they called it "burdens" (awzar) because it was sinful, since spoils were not yet lawful, or because they were under safe-conduct (musta'manin), and it is not permitted for one under safe-conduct to take the property of a belligerent. ﴿"So we threw it"﴾, i.e., into the fire.

﴿"Thus did al-Samiri cast"﴾, i.e., what he had with him of it.

It is related that when they thought the appointed period had been completed, al-Samiri said to them: "Musa has only broken his promise to you because of the ornaments of the people that you have with you, and they are unlawful for you. The opinion is that we dig a pit, kindle a fire in it, and throw into it everything we have." So they did so.

Abu 'Amr, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Abu Bakr and Rawh read ﴿حَمَلْنا﴾ (*hamalna*) with a fatha and without doubling the letter (*takhfif*).

﴿Then he brought forth for them a calf, a body﴾ from those melted ornaments. ﴿It had a lowing﴾, the sound of the calf. ﴿They said﴾, meaning al-Samiri and those who were seduced by him at the first sight of it: ﴿"This is your god and the god of Musa, but he has forgotten"﴾, i.e., Musa forgot him and went off seeking him at al-Tur. Or it means: al-Samiri forgot, i.e., he abandoned what he had been upon of showing faith.

﴿"Do they not see"﴾, i.e., do they not know? ﴿"that it does not return to them a word"﴾, that it does not return speech to them, nor give them a reply.

It is also read ﴿يَرْجِعَ﴾ (*yarji'a*) in the accusative, and this is weak, because *an* (أنّ) in its governing function (*al-nasiba*) does not occur after verbs of certainty (*af'al al-yaqin*). ﴿"And it has no power to harm them or benefit them"﴾, i.e., it has no ability to benefit or harm them.

﴿And Harun had already said to them before﴾ — before the return of Musa, peace be upon him; or before the words of the Samiri. Or it means: why did you not come after me and catch up with me? The particle "la" (lā, "not") is extra (māzidah, a grammatically superfluous particle), as in His words ﴿What prevented you from prostrating?﴾ ﴿Have you then disobeyed my command?﴾ by being steadfast in the religion and defending it.

﴿He said, "O son of my mother...﴾ He specified "mother" to appeal to his tenderness and gentleness. Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 95–96:

﴿He said, "What is your business, O Samiri?"﴾ That is: then he turned to him and said to him, disapprovingly, "What is your business?" That is, what is your aim in it, and what moved you to it? The word khatb is the verbal noun of khataba al-shay'a (he sought the matter), when one seeks it.

﴿He said, "I perceived what they did not perceive, so I took a handful from the footprint of the Messenger"﴾ Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read it with the ta' (tabsuru, "you perceive"), in the second person addressing them, meaning: I knew what you did not know and I grasped what you did not grasp, namely that the Messenger who came to you is spiritual, and that whatever his trace touches, he gives it life. Or: I saw what you did not see, namely that Jibril, upon him be blessings and peace, came to you upon the steed of life (faras al-hayah). It is said that he only recognized him because his mother cast him away at his birth out of fear of Pharaoh, and Jibril used to nourish him until he became independent. ﴿So I took a handful from the footprint of the Messenger﴾ from the dust of the place where he trod. The qabdah (handful) is a single act of grasping (al-qabd), and then the name is applied to what is grasped, like the Amir's "darb" (striking, i.e., the blow/what is struck). It is also read with the sad (qasdah), and the first (qabdah) is for taking with the whole palm, the second for taking with the tips of the fingers; and similar to them are khadm and qadm. The Messenger is Jibril, upon him be blessings and peace. Perhaps he did not name him because he did not know that he was Jibril, or he intended to draw attention to the time, which was when he was sent to him to take him to the Mount (Tur). ﴿So I threw it﴾ into the melted ornaments, or into the body of the calf, until it came alive. ﴿And thus my soul enticed me﴾ it adorned it for me and made it attractive to me.

He said, "Go, for in this life you will have a punishment for what you did," ﴿قالَ فاذْهَبْ فَإنَّ لَكَ في الحَياةِ﴾ punishment for what you did. ﴿أنْ تَقُولَ لا مِساسَ﴾ "That you say, 'No touching,'" out of fear that anyone would touch you, so that fever would seize you, and whoever touched you would be avoided by people, and they would avoid you, and you would be a banished, solitary outcast like a fleeing wild animal. It is also read "lā mussās" (لا مُسّاسَ) on the pattern of fujjār (كَفُجّارٍ), and it is a proper name for the act of touching.

﴿وَإنَّ لَكَ مَوْعِدًا﴾ "And you have an appointed time," in the Hereafter. ﴿لَنْ تُخْلَفَهُ﴾ "by which you will not be made to fail." God will not break it for you, and He will fulfill it for you in the Hereafter after punishing you in this world. Ibn Kathir and the two Basran readers (al-Basriyyān) read it with a kasra on the lām (لَنْ تُخْلِفَهُ), meaning: you will not fail to meet the one who made the promise to you, and it will surely come to you. The first object is omitted because the intended matter is the promise itself. It may also be from akhlaftu al-mawʿid (أخْلَفْتُ المَوْعِدَ), meaning when one finds the promise to be broken (khulf). It is also read with nūn (لَنُخْلِفَهُ), relating the words of God.

﴿وانْظُرْ إلى إلَهِكَ الَّذِي ظَلْتَ عَلَيْهِ عاكِفًا﴾ "And look at your god to which you remained devoted," ẓalilta ʿalayhi ʿākifan, meaning: you remained persistent in his worship. The first lām (ظَلْتَ, from ẓalilta) is dropped for lightness (takhfīf). It is also read with a kasra on the ẓāʾ (ظِلْتَ), by transferring the vowel of the lām to it. ﴿لَنُحَرِّقَنَّهُ﴾ "We will surely burn it," that is, with fire, and the reading ﴿لَنُحَرِّقَنَّهُ﴾ supports this. Or, with a file (al-mubarrad, الـمُبَرَّد), on the basis that it is an intensification (mubālaghah) of ḥaraqa, since it was made cool by filing. The reading ﴿لَنُحَرِّقَنَّهُ﴾ strengthens this.

﴿ثُمَّ لَنَنْسِفَنَّهُ﴾ "Then we will surely scatter it," meaning: then we will winnow it into ashes or filings. It is also read with a ḍamma on the sīn (لَنَنْضِفَنَّهُ / لَنُنْسِفَنَّهُ). ﴿فِي اليَمِّ نَسْفًا﴾ "into the sea, a scattering," so that nothing of it is found. The purpose of this is to increase his punishment and to show the foolishness of those who were captivated by him, to anyone who has even minimal insight.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 98:

(p-38)

﴿Indeed, your god is﴾ the one deserving of your worship. ﴿Allah, there is no god but He﴾, since no one resembles Him or comes near Him in perfection of knowledge and power. ﴿He has encompassed all things in knowledge﴾: His knowledge encompasses everything that can be known, not the calf which is fashioned and burned, even though it is alive in itself, and is a proverb for stupidity. It is also read as (wasi'a), and in that case the accusative of ﴿knowledge﴾ (ʿilman) is the object (maf'ul bihi), because although it is in the accusative of specification (tamyiz) in the well-known reading, it is in meaning the subject (fa'il). So when the verb is made transitive by doubling (ta'diya bi-l-tadif) to take two objects, it becomes an object.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 99:

﴿Thus﴾: like that narration (al-iqtisas), i.e., the narration of the story of Musa, peace be upon him. ﴿We relate to you some of the news of what has passed before﴾: from the reports of past matters and of the peoples who have gone by, as a lesson (tabsirah) for you, an increase in your knowledge, a multiplication of your miracles, and an admonition and reminder for those among your community who seek insight. ﴿And We have certainly given you from Us a reminder﴾: a Book comprising these narratives and reports, worthy of reflection and taking heed. The indefiniteness of "a reminder" here is for magnification. It has also been said that it means a good mention and a great renown among people.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verses 100–101:

﴿Whoever turns away from it﴾: from the Reminder (dhikr), which is the Qur'an, comprising all aspects of happiness and salvation. It has also been said that "it" refers to God.

﴿Then he will bear on the Day of Resurrection a burden (wizr)﴾: a heavy, crushing punishment for his disbelief, and for his sins, which he called a "burden" (wizr) by way of comparison, in respect of its weight upon the one who is punished and the difficulty of bearing it, to a load that weighs down the carrier and breaks his back. Or it means a great sin.

﴿Abiding therein﴾: in the burden, or in its carrying. The plural in "therein" and the singular in "turns away" are used in accordance with the sense and the wording (lafz).

﴿And evil will it be for them on the Day of Resurrection as a load﴾: that is, "how evil it is for them." In it there is an undefined pronoun (damir mubham) which is explained by "as a load" (himlan). The one being censured is omitted, meaning: "evil as a load is their burden." The lam in "for them" (lahum) is the lam of clarification (li'l-bayan), as in ﴿hayta laka﴾ (Qur'an 12:23). If you made sa'a (to be evil) mean "to grieve" (ahzana), and the pronoun in it referred to the burden (wizr), the matter of the lam and the accusative of "as a load" (himlan) would become problematic, and it would add no further meaning.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 102:

﴿On the Day the Trumpet is blown﴾. Abu 'Amr read it with a nun (nun), attributing the blowing to the One who commands it, as a mark of honour for Him or for the one who blows. It was also read with a fatha-vowelled ya (yaʼ), on the basis that the pronoun in it refers to God or to the pronoun of Israfil, even though his name has not been mentioned, because he is the one best known for this. It was also read as «fi al-suwar», which is the plural of ṣūrah (form), and its explanation has already been given before. ﴿And We shall gather the guilty on that Day, blue-eyed﴾. Blue-eyed (zuruq al-'uyun): they are described this way because blueness is the worst colour of the eye and the most hateful of them to the Arabs, since the Romans were their fiercest enemies and they had blue eyes. For this reason they used to describe the enemy as: "black-hearted, red-bearded, blue-eyed, or blind," for the pupil of a blind man becomes bluish.

﴿They whisper among themselves﴾: they lower their voices, because of the terror and dread that fill their hearts. Khafat (whispering) means lowering the voice and concealing it.

﴿You stayed only ten﴾: that is, in the world. They consider the duration of their stay there to be short, either because it has passed, or because the Hereafter seemed long to them, or out of regret over it when they witnessed the hardships and knew they deserved them for having squandered their lives on fulfilling desires and pursuing appetites. Or it refers to the grave, based on His saying: ﴿and on the day the Hour rises﴾, through to the end of the verses.

﴿We know best what they say﴾, which is the length of their stay. ﴿When the most exemplary of them in conduct says﴾: the most upright of them in opinion or in action. ﴿You stayed only a day﴾: an estimation (istirjah) of the saying of one who would be heavier in weight than them.(p-39)

And they ask you about the mountains. Its final outcome, and a man from the tribe of Thaqif had asked about them. ﴿Say﴾ to them: ﴿My Lord will blow them away with a blast﴾, He will make them like sand, then send winds upon them that scatter them.

﴿And He will leave it﴾, meaning He will leave their places of rest. Or it refers to the earth, and its pronoun is left unmentioned because the mountains indicate it, as in His saying: ﴿He leaves nothing upon its back of a creature﴾. ﴿A level plain﴾, empty, ﴿flat﴾, even, as if its parts were in one row.

﴿You will not see in it any crookedness or unevenness﴾, meaning no bending or protrusion, if you examine it by geometric measurement (al-qiyas al-handasi, geometric reckoning). These three are successive states: the first two are judged by perception, and the third by measurement. For this reason he mentioned ʿiwaj with a kasra (i.e., the form al-ʿiwaj, with the ʿayn vowelled with kasra), which is used specifically for abstract meanings, while al-amt, which is a slight protrusion, [is used for the physical]. It has also been said that ﴿you will not see﴾ is a resumed statement (istiʾnaf, a new independent clause) clarifying the two conditions.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 108–109:

﴿Upon that Day﴾ i.e., the Day when they are blown away (nusifat), with the day being added to the time of the blowing away. It is also permissible for it to be a second substitute (badal) for "the Day of Resurrection."

﴿They will follow the summoner﴾, the summoner of Allah to the place of gathering (al-mahshar). **Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verses 110–111:**

﴿He knows what is before them﴾: the circumstances that preceded them. ﴿And what is behind them﴾: what comes after them, which they will face. ﴿But they cannot encompass Him in knowledge﴾: their knowledge does not encompass His objects of knowledge. It has been said that it means His essence. It has also been said that the pronoun refers to one of the two relative clauses, or to both of them together. They did not know all of that, nor the details of what they did know of it.

﴿And faces will be humbled before the Living, the Self-Subsisting﴾: they will be abased and submit to Him with the submission of the ʿunāh (the captives, those in subjugation), who are the prisoners in the hand of a dominant, overpowering King. Its apparent meaning requires generality, though it is possible that it refers to the faces of the criminals, in which case the lām (the particle "to") replaces the idafah (the possessive construction), and this is supported by the context. ﴿And he has failed who bears wrongdoing﴾: this may be a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) or a resumptive new sentence (istiʾnāf), explaining what caused their faces to be humbled.

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on Surah 20, verses 120–122:**

﴿Then Satan whispered to him﴾: his whispering reached him. ﴿He said, "O Adam, shall I direct you to the tree of eternity (shajarat al-khuld) and a kingdom that does not decay?"﴾: the tree whose eater is made eternal and never dies at all. He attributed it to eternity (al-khuld), meaning everlasting life, because it is its cause according to his claim. ﴿And a kingdom that does not decay﴾: that does not cease and does not weaken.

﴿So they both ate from it, and their private parts became apparent to them, and they began to fasten over themselves some leaves of the Garden﴾: they began to stick the leaves over their private parts for concealment, and it was fig leaves. ﴿And Adam disobeyed his Lord﴾: by eating from the tree. ﴿And he went astray﴾: he strayed from the sought objective and failed, in that he sought eternity by eating from the tree; or from what he was commanded; or from right guidance, in that he was deceived by the words of the enemy. It was also read as "fa-ghawa" from "ghawa al-fasil," when the weaned young camel has been overfed with milk. The reproach upon him with disobedience and error, despite the slightness of his lapse, is a magnification of the lapse and a powerful deterrent to his descendants from it.

﴿Then his Lord chose him﴾: He selected him and brought him near by inclining him to repentance and enabling him to it, from "ajba ila kadha" (to be drawn to such a thing), as in "ajtabaytuhu," like "jaliytu 'ala al-arus fajtalaytuha" (I unveiled the bride, and so I unveiled her); the root meaning of the word is gathering. ﴿So He accepted his repentance﴾: He accepted his repentance when he repented. ﴿And guided him﴾: to steadfastness in repentance and clinging to the means of protection (from sin).
