Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 130:

﴿So be patient over what they say, and glorify the praise of your Lord﴾: and pray while praising your Lord for His guidance and His enabling you (to it). Or, declare Him free of partners (shirk) and of all the deficiencies they attribute to Him, praising Him for having distinguished you with guidance, acknowledging that He is the Master of all blessings. ﴿Before the rising of the sun﴾: meaning the Fajr (dawn prayer). ﴿And before its setting﴾: meaning the Zuhr (noon prayer) and the 'Asr (afternoon prayer), because they fall at the end of the day, or the 'Asr alone.

﴿And during the hours of the night﴾: and during its periods. (The word) āna is the plural of ānin (with a kasra and short vowel), or of anā' (with a fatha and a long vowel). ﴿Then glorify (Him)﴾: meaning the Maghrib (sunset prayer) and the 'Isha' (night prayer). The time of night is mentioned first because of its specific excellence, for the heart is most gathered in it and the self is most inclined to rest, so worship in it is more arduous. For this reason the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, the rising at night is firmer in tread and more upright in speech﴾. ﴿And at the extremities of the day﴾: a repetition (of the mention) of the Subh (dawn) and Maghrib prayers, intending to specify them. Its being expressed in the plural form is because there is no risk of confusion, as in his saying:

"Their two backs are like the backs of two shields"

Or it is a command to (perform) the Zuhr prayer, for it is the end of the first half of the day and the beginning of the second half; its being in the plural is in consideration of the two halves, or because "the day" is a genus, or (it refers to) voluntary prayer in the parts of the day. ﴿That you may be pleased﴾: this is connected to "glorify" (sabbih), meaning: glorify (Him) at these times, in the hope that you will attain from God that by which you will please your self. Al-Kisa'i and Abu Bakr read it in the passive voice, meaning: your Lord will please you.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 131:

﴿And do not extend your eyes﴾ meaning: the gaze of your eyes. ﴿toward that with which We have provided enjoyment﴾, admiring it and wishing that you had the like of it. ﴿as pairs from among them﴾ and kinds from among the disbelievers. It is permissible for it to be a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative) from the pronoun in bihi (“with it”), with the object being “from among them,” meaning: toward that which We have provided enjoyment with, namely the kinds of some of them, or some people among them. ﴿the splendour of the life of this world﴾ is in the accusative by an elided verb indicated by ﴿We have provided enjoyment﴾, or by ﴿with it﴾ on the basis of it being understood to contain the meaning of “We have given,” or in apposition (badal) to the place of ﴿with it﴾, or in apposition to ﴿pairs﴾ with an elided genitive governing word (muḍāf) or without one, or it is in the accusative of dispraise. It means adornment and radiance. Yaʿqūb read it with a fatḥah (zahratu), and it is a dialect form like jahrah in al-jahrah (“openly”). Or it is the plural of zāhir, serving as a description of them, meaning that they flaunt the world because of their luxury and the splendour of their appearance, unlike the ascetic believers. ﴿that We may test them thereby﴾: that We may try them and examine them through it, or that We may punish them in the Hereafter because of it. ﴿But the provision of your Lord﴾: what He has stored up for you in the Hereafter, or what He has provided you of guidance and prophethood. ﴿is better﴾ than what He granted them in this world, ﴿and more lasting﴾, for it does not come to an end.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 132:

﴿And enjoin prayer upon your family, and be steadfast in it.﴾ He was commanded to order the people of his household, or those among his community who follow him, to perform prayer after he himself had been commanded to do so, so that they would help one another by seeking aid through it in their needs, and would not be preoccupied with matters of livelihood nor turn their attention to it the way the people of wealth do. ﴿And be steadfast in it﴾: persist in it and maintain it. ﴿We do not ask you for provision﴾: that you should provide for yourself or for your family. ﴿We provide for you﴾ and for them, so free your mind for the affair of the Hereafter. ﴿And the good end﴾: the praiseworthy outcome ﴿is for righteousness﴾: for those who possess taqwa (God-consciousness).

It is narrated that "whenever harm befell his family, he (ﷺ) would command them to pray and would recite this verse."

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 133:**

﴿They say: "Why does he not bring us a sign from his Lord?"﴾ A sign (*ayah*) that would indicate the truth of his claim to prophethood (*nubuwwah*), or a sign of their own choosing, as a denial of the signs that he brought, or as a dismissal of them, out of obstinacy and stubbornness. So God silenced them by pointing to the Qur'an, which is the mother of miracles (*mu'jizat*), the greatest of them and the most lasting. This is because the reality of a miracle is that the one who claims prophethood is singled out with a kind of knowledge or action in a way that breaks the normal course of things. There is no doubt that knowledge is the root of action, higher in rank than it and more lasting in its effect. Thus, whatever is of this kind is likewise. He also drew their attention to a clearer aspect of the miraculous character specific to this subject, saying: ﴿Has there not come to them the clear evidence of what is in the earlier scriptures?﴾ That is, of the Torah, the Gospel and the rest of the heavenly books. Its containing the essence of their beliefs and general rulings, while the one who brought it is unlettered (*ummi*), who had not read them and had not learned from anyone who knew them, is a manifest miracle. It also implies that, just as it proves his prophethood, it is a proof for the books that came before it, in that it is miraculous, whereas those books are not like that; rather, they depend on something that attests to their authenticity.

The reading *al-Suhuf* (الصُّحُفِ) is also recited with the lightened form. Nafi', Abu 'Amr and Hafs, on the authority of 'Asim, read ﴿Has there not come to them﴾ with the *ta'* (تَأْتِهِمْ), and the rest read it with the *ya'* (يَأْتِهِمْ).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verses 134–135:

﴿And had We destroyed them with a punishment before it﴾, before Muhammad (ﷺ), or before the clear sign and the reminder, because it is in the sense of the proof. Or what is meant by it is the Qur'an. ﴿They would have said, "Our Lord, why did You not send to us a messenger so that we might follow Your signs before we are humbled"﴾ by being killed and taken captive in this world. ﴿And disgraced﴾ by entering the Fire on the Day of Resurrection. It has been read in the passive voice in both places.

﴿Say, "Each"﴾, meaning each one of us and of you, ﴿is waiting﴾, awaiting what our affair and your affair will come to. ﴿So wait﴾. It was also read as "so enjoy" (fatamatta'u). ﴿Then you will know who are the companions of the upright path﴾, the straight one. It was read as al-sawa' (the middle, good path), and as al-su'a and al-su' (evil). Al-suwayy is its diminutive. ﴿And who is guided﴾ from misguidance. Man (who) in both places is interrogative, and its position in i'rab (grammatical analysis) is nominative, as the subject of a nominal sentence. It is permissible for the second man to be relative, unlike the first, due to the absence of a returning pronoun. In that case it is coordinated with the place of the interrogative clause, whose verb is suspended (mu'allaq), on the basis that knowledge means cognizance, or on the basis of "companions of," or on "the path," on the understanding that what is meant by it is the Prophet (ﷺ).

And from him (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Ta-Ha will be given, on the Day of Resurrection, the reward of the Emigrants and the Helpers, may God be pleased with them all."
